nodes.content: What do you want to do today?
Which book contains the final word of God?
Did Joseph Smith restore the true church?

edges.label: Time
edges.explanation: Everyone uses seconds, minutes and hours; s is the SI base unit.

edges.label: Electric current
edges.explanation: The ampere is the SI base unit; small currents use mA.

edges.label: Amount of substance
edges.explanation: Chemists count particles in moles: one mole is about 6.022 × 10²³ of them.

edges.label: A physics or chemistry formula
edges.explanation: Gas laws, radiation and efficiencies need zero at absolute zero, so use kelvin.

edges.label: The colour of light
edges.explanation: Bulbs and screens give colour temperature in kelvin: 2700 K is warm white.

edges.label: Very cold things or space
edges.explanation: Cryogenics and astronomy work near absolute zero, where kelvin reads naturally.

edges.label: A lab reading or a change
edges.explanation: Labs and engineers use °C. A change of 1 °C is the same as a change of 1 K.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Daily life uses °F; scientists use °C and K.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Forecasts, ovens and doctors use °C.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Weather uses °C, though many ovens are marked in °F.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: Daily use leans to °F, but sources conflict.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Forecasts use °C.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Forecasts use °F; the Bahamas and Belize also use °C.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses °C.

edges.label: Aircraft altitude
edges.explanation: Aviation gives altitude in feet almost everywhere; China and a few others use metres.

edges.label: Distance at sea or in the air
edges.explanation: A nautical mile is 1852 m, about one minute of latitude.

edges.label: Screens, wheels or pipes
edges.explanation: Screen sizes, wheel rims and pipe threads are in inches worldwide.

edges.label: Distances in the solar system
edges.explanation: 1 au is the mean Earth–Sun distance; the SI accepts it.

edges.label: Stars and galaxies, for astronomers
edges.explanation: Research papers use parsecs (kpc, Mpc).

edges.label: Stars and galaxies, for everyone
edges.explanation: Popular writing uses light-years.

edges.label: Atoms and crystals
edges.explanation: Crystallographers and chemists use Å; 1 Å = 0.1 nm.

edges.label: Light waves and microchips
edges.explanation: Wavelengths and chip features are given in nm.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: Use the metre with prefixes (mm, km); engineering drawings use mm.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Road signs and maps use miles.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Road signs must use miles and yards.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Road signs have used km since the 1970s.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: People still talk in miles, though new speed limits use km/h.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Road signs show miles, though speed limits are in km/h.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Road signs use miles.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses km.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Height is given in feet and inches.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Most people use feet and inches; doctors record cm.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: About 80% of Canadians give height in feet and inches (2022 poll).

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: US customary units are the norm.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Sources are thin; feet and inches are common from British-era use.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Feet and inches are the norm.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses cm.

edges.label: Food at the shop or market
Gold or silver
edges.explanation: Precious metals trade in troy ounces (31.1 g), even in metric countries.

edges.label: Gems
edges.explanation: One carat is 200 mg.

edges.label: Cargo or freight
edges.explanation: World trade uses the tonne (1000 kg); US domestic freight uses short tons.

edges.label: Atoms or molecules
edges.explanation: 1 Da is one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom; biochemists use kDa for proteins.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: The kilogram is the SI base unit.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Body weight is given in pounds.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Most adults use stones and pounds; the NHS records kg.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: About 76% of Canadians use pounds (2022 poll).

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: US customary units are the norm.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Sources are thin; pounds are also used.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Pounds are the norm.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses kg.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Prices and labels use pounds and ounces.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Shops must price in metric; loose goods may also show pounds.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Labels are metric, though prices are often also shown per pound.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: US customary units are the norm, with metric in some shops.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Markets weigh food in viss (about 1.6 kg) and ticals (1/100 viss).

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Shops price in pounds.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses kg and g.

edges.label: Draught beer in the UK or Ireland
edges.explanation: UK law keeps the pint for draught beer and cider; a pint is 568 mL.

edges.label: Crude oil
edges.explanation: Oil trades in barrels of 42 US gallons (159 L).

edges.label: A US or Canadian recipe
edges.explanation: Recipes use cups (240 mL), tablespoons and teaspoons.

edges.label: Any other recipe
edges.explanation: Most recipes use mL; a teaspoon is 5 mL, a tablespoon 15 mL (20 mL in Australia).

edges.label: Drinks or containers
edges.explanation: Bottles and cartons are sold in litres and mL; the US also uses fl oz.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: The cubic metre is the SI unit; chemists use L and mL.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Pumps sell US gallons (3.79 L).

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Pumps sell litres, but fuel economy is quoted in miles per gallon.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Pumps sell litres.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: Fuel is sold in US gallons.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Fuel is sold by the gallon.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Belize uses US gallons; the Cayman Islands use imperial gallons (4.55 L).

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses litres.

edges.label: Aircraft, ships or wind at sea
edges.explanation: One knot is one nautical mile per hour.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: m/s is the SI unit.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Speed limits are in mph.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Speed limits must be in mph.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Speed limits are in km/h.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: Speed limits are now in km/h.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Speed limits are in km/h by law, though distances are in miles.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Speed limits are in mph.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses km/h.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: The square metre is the SI unit; the SI also accepts the hectare.

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Land is sold in acres.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Land is still quoted in acres, though official records use hectares.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Farmland is quoted in acres.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: Land is sold in acres.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Farmland is measured in acres.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Land is sold in acres.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses hectares; 1 ha is 10,000 m².

edges.label: United States
edges.explanation: Listings use square feet.

edges.label: United Kingdom
edges.explanation: Listings show both; many buyers think in square feet.

edges.label: Canada
edges.explanation: Listings use square feet.

edges.label: Liberia
edges.explanation: US customary units are the norm.

edges.label: Myanmar
edges.explanation: Condos are marketed in square feet.

edges.label: Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands
edges.explanation: Listings use square feet.

edges.label: Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands
edges.explanation: These countries follow US practice.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: The rest of the world uses m².

edges.label: Food
edges.explanation: Labels show kcal (US: 'Calories'); the EU adds kJ, and Australia and New Zealand put kJ first.

edges.label: Electricity or gas bills
edges.explanation: Bills use kWh; US gas bills use therms instead.

edges.label: US heating or air conditioning
edges.explanation: US furnaces and air conditioners are rated in BTU per hour.

edges.label: Particles or atoms
edges.explanation: Particle and atomic physics use eV (keV, MeV, GeV).

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: The joule is the SI unit.

edges.label: A car engine
edges.explanation: Adverts use hp (or PS in Europe); EU specs must also give kW.

edges.label: Electrical devices or power plants
edges.explanation: Use W, with kW for appliances and MW for power plants.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: The watt is the SI unit.

edges.label: Blood pressure
edges.explanation: Doctors everywhere use mmHg.

edges.label: Weather, outside the US
edges.explanation: Forecasts use hPa, which equals the millibar.

edges.label: Weather, in the US
edges.explanation: US forecasts and altimeters use inches of mercury.

edges.label: Diving or gas cylinders
edges.explanation: Divers outside the US use bar; US divers use psi.

edges.label: Science or engineering
edges.explanation: The pascal is the SI unit; engineers often use kPa or MPa.

edges.label: Continental Europe
edges.explanation: Gauges and door stickers show bar first.

edges.label: Elsewhere
edges.explanation: Gauges show psi; many also show bar.

edges.label: How bright a lamp is
edges.explanation: Bulb packs give total light output in lumens.

edges.label: How bright a surface is
edges.explanation: Workplace and photography guides give lux (lumens per m²).

edges.label: Brightness in one direction
edges.explanation: The candela is the SI base unit, used for LEDs and headlamps.
